newsitem.title: USA: Studies show botched prescriptions in U.S. hospitals.
newsitem.headline: Studies show botched prescriptions in U.S. hospitals.

text.p: Adverse drug reactions caused by botched prescriptions in U.S. hospitals are needlessly harming patients and adding to health care costs, according to studies published on Tuesday.
"Adverse drug reactions in hospitals are common, costly and preventable in many cases," said Jerry Avon of Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston.

"Whatever the precise measure of their impact, their toll in human and fiscal terms is clearly large enough to justify commitment of hospital resources to programs designed to reduce (them) to the lowest possible incidence," he said in an editorial in this week's Journal of the American Medical Association.
The journal published a series of reports on the problem.

In one study, doctors at LDS Hospital in Salt Lake City said cases wherein the wrong drugs are prescribed or ordered in incorrect doses may nearly double the risk of death among affected hospitalized patients.
A second report from Albany Medical Center found an error rate of nearly four out of every 1,000 medication orders.

Common mistakes included prescribing drugs about which the doctor knew too little and the failure to recognize problems in patients -- such as allergies, age or physical conditions -- that may have made the drugs inappropriate, the second study said.
A third study from Brigham and Women's Hospital of more than 4,000 patients over a six-month period found there were 190 adverse drug reactions, of which 60 could have been prevented.
